restrictR

the same input check, written once

restrictR checks the arguments of R functions against contracts, such as “a single non-negative number” or “a data frame with numeric columns x1 and x2”, that are written once and called at the top of every function that takes the argument.

A contract is built with the base pipe: restrict() names the argument and each require_*() step adds one check. The result is a validator, an ordinary R function that stops with a message of the form path: message when a value fails. Each pipe returns a new validator and leaves the one it started from unchanged, so a shared base can be extended in several directions. You decide which contracts share a base and where each validator is called. restrictR supports:

  • One rule for many functions. A validator defined once is called by every function that takes the same argument, so the rule and its error message live in one place.
  • Rules that depend on other arguments. A one-sided formula such as ~ nrow(newdata) refers to another argument, which is passed to the validator when it is called.
  • Errors that point to the value. A failure names the path to the offending element (newdata$x2), what was expected and what was found, with the positions of missing values.
  • Contracts as documentation. A validator prints its steps as a numbered list, and as_contract_text() renders them as text for a roxygen @param.
  • Checks without stopping. is_valid() returns TRUE or FALSE, validation_errors() returns the messages, and expect_valid() and expect_invalid() test a validator with testthat.

restrictR is written in base R and imports no other package.

Installation 

install.packages("restrictR")

Development version:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/restrictR")

Usage

  1. Name the argument with restrict().
  2. Add one require_*() step per condition with |>.
  3. Call the validator at the top of each function that takes the argument.
library(restrictR)

require_dose <- restrict("dose") |>
  require_numeric() |>
  require_length(1L) |>
  require_positive()

require_dose(2.5)
require_dose(-1)
#> Error:
#> ! dose: must be non-negative
#>   Found: -1

A value that passes returns invisibly, so the call prints nothing. A value that fails stops with the argument name, the condition and the value found.

One rule for many functions

A contract for a data frame combines steps on the whole object with validators for single columns:

require_feature <- restrict("feature") |>
  require_numeric(no_na = TRUE, finite = TRUE)

require_newdata <- restrict("newdata") |>
  require_df() |>
  require_has_cols(c("x1", "x2")) |>
  require_col("x1", require_feature) |>
  require_col("x2", require_feature) |>
  require_nrow_min(1L)

require_newdata(data.frame(x1 = 1:3, x2 = c("a", "b", "c")))
#> Error:
#> ! newdata$x2: must be numeric, got character

predict(), simulate() or any other function that takes newdata calls require_newdata(newdata) as its first line. A change to the rule is made once, in the definition.

Rules that depend on other arguments

A one-sided formula names another argument, and that argument is passed to the validator by name when it is called:

require_pred <- restrict("pred") |>
  require_numeric(no_na = TRUE) |>
  require_length_matches(~ nrow(newdata))

newdata <- data.frame(x1 = 1:3, x2 = c(0.5, 1.5, 2.5))
require_pred(c(0.1, 0.2), newdata = newdata)
#> Error:
#> ! pred: length must match nrow(newdata) (3)
#>   Found: length 2

The validator reads newdata only from its arguments, never from the calling environment.

A validator that documents itself

Printing a validator lists its steps, and as_contract_text() turns the same list into the text of a roxygen @param, so the documentation of an argument follows its contract:

require_newdata
#> <restriction newdata>
#>   1. must be a data.frame
#>   2. must have columns: "x1", "x2"
#>   3. $x1: must be numeric, no NA, finite
#>   4. $x2: must be numeric, no NA, finite
#>   5. must have at least 1 row
#' @param newdata `r as_contract_text(require_newdata)`

require_custom() adds a step with a check of your own, reported in the same format through fail(). The reference index lists every built-in step, grouped into type, missingness, structure, value, character, file-system and function checks.

Compared with checkmate

checkmate provides assert*(), check*() and test*() functions in C that are called inline, one per argument, where the check is needed. restrictR names a contract once, reuses it across functions, and prints it as documentation. The two work together: a require_custom() step can call a checkmate assertion. Relation to checkmate compares them further.

Getting help

Questions and bug reports go to the GitHub issues. A bug report is easiest to act on with a small reproducible example, for instance made with reprex.
